newsitem.title: CHINA: China leaders worry about population, environment.
newsitem.headline: China leaders worry about population, environment.

text.p: China, home to one-fifth of humanity, has sounded alarm bells over its growing masses, saying overpopulation is driving people into poverty and ruining the environment, the Xinhua news agency said on Thursday.

Although China's once-strict family planning policies had succeeded in checking population growth in the past few years, much work was still needed to meet future goals, Xinhua quoted President Jiang Zemin as saying.

"The over-population warning must be sounded constantly and continued efforts must be made to guarantee that China controls its population within 1.3 billion by the end of this century," Xinhua quoted Jiang as saying in a March speech.

China is the world's most populous nation with 1.224 billion people at the end of 1996, up 12.68 million from the year before and with a natural population growth rate of 10.42 per 1,000, latest official figures show.

Beijing's one couple, one child family planning policy launched in the late 1970s largely succeeded in reining in a population that had swelled under the rule of Chairman Mao Zedong, who believed a large population would make China powerful.
But family planning programmes have gradually lost their effectiveness after nearly two decades of economic reform have loosened state control over people's lives.
"Family planning work is arduous and must not be slackened at any time," Jiang said, adding that China's poor regions could enrich themselves by checking their populations.
"One of the major reasons for the underdevelopment of poverty-stricken areas is that the population growth in those areas is too fast," Jiang said.
Those poor areas that did a good job of family planning work should be given preference in handing out poverty relief funds, technical training and in resettlement programmes, Jiang said.
Jiang said overpopulation, coupled with breakneck economic growth, had caused serious environmental damage and said China needed to improve a legal framework to help protect the ecology.
"Any relaxation in our efforts to protect the environment would lead to an increase in the volume of discharged pollutants and in the scale of ecosystem damage," Jiang said.

Premier Li Peng joined Jiang in the call to step up the fight against pollution, saying acid rain now plagued some Chinese cities and that urban drinking water supplies were threatened with serious contamination.
"The general environmental quality has continued to deteriorate," Xinhua quoted Li as saying. "China still faces a heavy task to bring a fairly good environment to the 21st century."
Beijing had earmarked 450 billion yuan ($54.22 billion) for environmental protection in the five years from 1996-2000, Li said but gave no details on how the money would be spent.
China should not sacrifice its environmental health for short-term economic gain, Li said.
"China must not follow the old road of 'pollution control after pollution'," he said.
